title: EU publishes first European standard to support the Cyber Resilience Act
excerpt: The first standard for the EU's connected-product security law sets shared terms and lifecycle security steps, from design to end of support. More than 30 others are on the way.

sources.title: European Commission: First European standard published to support the Cyber Resilience Act
Poland Insight: EU releases first Cyber Resilience Act standards

body_html:
The European Union's law on the security of connected products has its first supporting European standard. The European Commission said on 19 November 2026 that the standard was published on 18 November by the European standards organisations, and described the step as "a signal that the CRA standards framework is becoming operational".

The Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) sets security rules for "products with digital elements": almost anything with software that connects to a device or a network. The Commission's examples include connected door locks, home routers, microcontrollers, operating systems, web browsers and password managers, along with cloud functions that a product depends on.

What the standard covers

The Commission said the new standard sets out general cybersecurity principles for these products across their whole life: design, development, production, maintenance, the end of support and final decommissioning. It is meant to help manufacturers organise their security work in a way that is more systematic and easier to audit.

According to Poland Insight's report on the announcement by CEN and CENELEC, two of Europe's official standards bodies, the work comes in two parts:

  • EN 40000-1-1, a shared vocabulary, so that makers, testers and regulators use the same terms.
  • EN 40000-1-2, principles for managing cybersecurity risk and the security activities expected at each stage of a product's life, including end of support and retirement.

The Commission's own page speaks of "the first standard" and does not give the numbers, so readers should check the final titles with the standards bodies.

What it does not do yet

Under EU product law, a manufacturer that follows a "harmonised" standard can be presumed to meet the matching legal requirements. That only happens once the standard's reference is published in the EU's Official Journal. Poland Insight reported that, as of 19 November 2026, this had not been confirmed. Until it is, manufacturers can use the standard to build their processes and documentation, but it does not by itself show that a product complies.

The Commission said more than 30 standards are being written. It asked CEN, CENELEC and ETSI for them in February 2025. Standards for specific product categories will build on this general one.

Key dates

  • 11 September 2026: manufacturers' duty to report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents began to apply, as reported by Poland Insight.
  • 11 December 2027: the CRA applies in full.

Why it matters for staying in charge

A home robot, a smart lock or an AI device is only as trustworthy as the software behind it. Shared rules for how makers handle security from first design to the last update support Directive 6, Secure and supported, and Directive 10, Safe for its whole life. Clear, auditable processes also make it easier to see who answers for a product, which is the point of Directive 9, Accountable.

For buyers, the practical question stays the same: how long will this product get security updates, and how will the maker tell me when they stop? A hacked robot is one nobody is in charge of. More on that on our security page.
